item.statement_excerpt:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Sigma$ be a closed connected Riemann surface, $X=\operatorname{Sym}^m(\Sigma)$ with its standard complex structure, and $m\ge1$. For $a\in\Sigma$ put $E_a=\{a\}+\operatorname{Sym}^{m-1}(\Sigma)$. This is a smooth complex hypersurface, including at repeated tuples. The universal incidence hypersurface $\mathcal E=\{(a,D):D\in E_a\}\subset\Sigma\times X$ carries a smooth complex divisor line bundle with its canonical section, whose zero set is $\mathcal E$ with multiplicity one.

For a smooth map $v:S\to X$, where $S$ is an oriented sphere or a closed disk, define $n_a(v)$ as the degree of the pullback point-divisor line bundle; for a disk use the canonical section to trivialize it on the boundary, and require $v(\partial S)\cap E_a=\varnothing$. The proof constructs this integer by elementary frame winding. It is defined even when a sphere lies wholly in $E_a$.

For a sphere, $n_a(v)$ is independent of $a$ on all of $\Sigma$. For a disk whose boundary tuples have all entries in a finite union of curves $\Gamma\subset\Sigma$, it is independent of $a$ on each connected component of $\Sigma\setminus\Gamma$. If $v^{-1}(E_a)$ is finite and the map is holomorphic on a neighborhood of every one of these points, then
$$n_a(v)=\sum_{z\in v^{-1}(E_a)}\operatorname{ord}_z(F_a\circ v)\ge0,$$
where $F_a$ is any local holomorphic defining function of the smooth hypersurface $E_a$. Each term is a positive integer. Thus the degree agrees with proper holomorphic intersection multiplicity, while divisor containment is handled by its degree definition and actual point movement rather than an unsupported proper-intersection assumption.

proof_step_donor_fragments.exact_current_text: Near $(a_0,D_0)\in\mathcal E$ choose one small complex disk about $a_0$ containing exactly the cluster of tuple entries equal to $a_0$, and disjoint disks about the other support points. Let $P_D(T)$ be the monic cluster polynomial in the corresponding symmetric-function coordinates. For $a$ close to $a_0$, the incidence condition is exactly $P_D(a)=0$. The derivative with respect to its constant coefficient is one. Thus this is a smooth complex hypersurface even when $a$ is a multiple root; it also shows that $D'\mapsto a+D'$ embeds $\operatorname{Sym}^{m-1}\Sigma$ holomorphically onto $E_a$. Local defining functions for this hypersurface have nonzero holomorphic ratios on overlaps. To verify extension of a ratio across its apparent zero set, use one definer as the transverse coordinate $t$ by [F1]; the other is $t h$ by integrating its transverse derivative from $0$ to $t$, and $h$ is holomorphic and nonzero there because both definers have nonzero transverse differential. These extended ratios satisfy the cocycle identity, since it holds off the hypersurface and then by continuity. Define a complex line bundle by local frames $e_i$ with $e_j=(F_i/F_j)e_i$. The local sections $F_i e_i$ agree, and give its canonical section. Away from incidence take a definer equal to one, so the construction covers all of $\Sigma\times X$. This constructs the actual divisor line bundle and section, not merely their formal names. [F1, construct, algebra]

We recall with a direct construction the elementary line-bundle degree needed here. A smooth complex line bundle over a disk has a smooth nowhere-zero frame. Embed it in a trivial finite-dimensional complex bundle by a finite local partition and its local frames, take the smooth Hermitian projection $Q(z)$ onto its image, and transport a basis at the disk center along each radius with $W_\lambda=[Q_\lambda,Q]W$, $W(0)=I$. The iterated-integral series converges with bound $M^n/n!$ for its length-$n$ term, and fixed parameter derivatives have the same factorial bound times a polynomial in $n$. It is smooth and unique; $W^*W=I$ and $(W^{-1}QW)_\lambda=0$, by $Q^2=Q$. Thus it transports a nonzero vector to a smooth frame. On an oriented sphere choose two closed hemispheres with a collar overlap and frames $e_N,e_S$. Write $e_S=g e_N$ on the positively oriented equator of the north hemisphere and define the degree as $\operatorname{wind}g$. A change of either disk frame multiplies $g$ by the boundary value of a nonzero disk function or its inverse, so [F2] makes that degree independent of these frames. On a disk with a section $\sigma$ nonzero on its boundary, write $\sigma=f e$ in a disk frame and define its relative degree as $\operatorname{wind}(f|_{\partial S})$, likewise independent of the frame. All windings here have the normalization $(2\pi i)^{-1}\int f^{-1}df$ with the specified boundary orientation. [F2, construct, algebra]

Degree is invariant in the required actual families, including when a section becomes identically zero. A smooth line bundle over $[0,1]\times S$ has a finite local complex embedding into a trivial Hermitian bundle over that compact base, by the same finite partition construction as step 1.2. Its image projection $Q(t,z)$ is smooth. The specified series for $W_t=[Q_t,Q]W$ with $W(0,z)=I$ gives a global smooth complex isomorphism between the endpoint bundles, and indeed identifies every parameter fiber with the first one. The same skew-Hermitian and projection computation in step 1.2 proves this, and compactness gives the uniform derivative bounds for the series. Transport hemisphere frames along these identifications; their clutch transition is unchanged, so the sphere degree is constant. In the disk case transport one disk frame; if its given boundary section stays nonzero, its boundary component is a smooth homotopy of nonzero loops and its winding is constant by [F2]. Thus relative degree is constant as well. This parameter identification applies also to pullbacks by smooth source isotopies, without assuming that the particular canonical section has isolated zeros. [F2, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

For a smooth section with finitely many isolated zeros, these degrees equal the sum of its local winding indices. On a framed disk remove disjoint small disks about its zeros. The form $f^{-1}df$ is closed on the remaining region, because $d(f^{-1}df)=-f^{-2}df\wedge df=0$. Integrating it gives outer boundary winding equal to the sum of the small positively oriented inner-circle windings. This use of the planar Stokes formula follows directly by a finite coordinate partition and the two one-variable fundamental theorems; no global selection theorem is needed. Apply it on both hemispheres of a sphere, with no zero on their common circle. The equator contributions differ by $\operatorname{wind}g$ since the southern boundary orientation is opposite, so their total zero index is the degree in step 1.2. The circle can always be moved off the finite zeros by a small smooth rotation. The degree does not change during such a rotation: pull the bundle back by that source isotopy, and identify the resulting family of bundles by the projection transport in step 2.1, or directly the same commutator series in its parameter. The clutch windings are integer and continuous. This also verifies independence from the chosen hemisphere cut. For completeness any line bundle admits a section with isolated zeros: on the northern equatorial collar let $M(z)=z^k$ if its transition winding $k$ is nonnegative, and $M(z)=\overline z^{-k}$ if $k<0$. The quotient of the full collar transition by $M$ has zero winding and has a nonzero relative collar extension $A$ by [F2]. Then the northern coefficient $MA$ agrees with that full transition on a smaller collar and glues with the constant southern coefficient one. It is smooth and has its only possible zero at the northern center. The relative extension preserves all collar derivatives. The zero-sum characterization therefore makes the same degree independent of the chosen cut for arbitrary line bundles as well. [F2, step 1.2, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

Apply these constructions to the pullback of the actual universal divisor bundle of step 1.1 by $(a,v(z))$. On the sphere take the absolute degree in step 1.2, which is defined for every $a$, even for an identically zero canonical section. For two points $a_0,a_1$ choose a smooth path in the connected Riemann surface $\Sigma$; one exists by a finite chain of coordinate disks and smoothing polygonal segments. Its pullback gives the smooth family in step 2.1, proving $n_{a_0}(v)=n_{a_1}(v)$. On the disk, every $a$ outside $\Gamma$ makes the canonical boundary section nonzero, since a boundary tuple contains no point outside $\Gamma$. Two points in the same connected component can be joined by such a smooth path staying there, so step 2.1 proves the asserted relative invariance. This is the point-movement argument even when the original sphere was wholly inside a point divisor. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

Finally suppose the inverse image of $E_a$ is finite and the map is holomorphic near it. In each local bundle frame its canonical section component is $F_a\circ v$ times a nonzero smooth frame factor; use its defining holomorphic frame to compute the winding. By [F1] its germ is $z^r h(z)$ with $r\ge1$ and $h$ nonzero on a small disk. Its local winding is $r$, because the nonzero factor has zero boundary winding by [F2]. Frame changes do not change that local integer. Step 3.1 now sums those integers to the absolute or relative degree just constructed. They are precisely the proper holomorphic intersection multiplicities, and their sum is nonnegative. Containment itself was not treated as a proper intersection: its degree was defined first, and only a justified point move to a proper divisor can subsequently compute it by this formula. All constructions used finite local charts, explicit matrix series and one-variable winding under Countable Choice. [F1, F2, step 3.1, step 3.2, construct, algebra] ∎
